Volume 12 · Chapter 02

Linear models and robust inference

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c01

By the endDerive linear estimators and choose inference appropriate to dependence and heterogeneity.

Volume 12 · Chapter 2

Linear models and robust inference

A regression can be a well-defined description of a population, an unbiased estimator under a conditional model, or a basis for asymptotic inference. These are different achievements. A covariance estimator that allows unequal variances does not identify a causal effect. A thousand measurements of the same common shock do not constitute a thousand independent shocks. Changing regression weights can change the population question as well as the precision of its answer.

Capability. Derive population and sample projections, exact OLS and known-covariance GLS results, and justified covariance estimators for three explicit sampling structures: iid observations, iid bounded-size clusters, and bounded stationary finite-range dependence. Diagnose rank, leverage, misspecified weights, dependence and finite-sample inference failures. All numerical cases and exercises are original synthetic examples; currency amounts are generic currency units (CU), not market observations.

Prerequisites. Chapter 1 supplies stochastic orders, finite-dimensional iid score limits, continuous inversion and studentization. Matrix projections and positive-definite square roots come from Volume 2, Chapter 6 and Chapter 10. The smooth replacement proof of the scalar iid CLT is in Volume 3, Chapter 6; we extend that argument explicitly to the bounded dependent case below. No general mixing CLT, high-dimensional approximation or arbitrary estimated-covariance theorem is assumed.

1. Projection is a target before it is an algorithm

Let y be a scalar outcome and x a p-dimensional column of regressors. Dimension p is fixed throughout the chapter. A prime means transpose. Assume E[y²]<∞, E‖x‖²<∞ and Q=E[xx′] positive definite. The best linear projection coefficient minimizes the population squared prediction loss, not necessarily a structural economic loss:

β=argminb∈ℝᵖ E[(y−x′b)²]=Q−1E[xy],
e=y−x′β, E[xe]=0.

Cauchy–Schwarz makes E[xy] finite. Expanding around β gives E[(y−x′b)²]=E[e²]+(b−β)′Q(b−β), because the cross term is zero. Positive definiteness proves existence and uniqueness. Orthogonality means the zero cross moments E[xⱼe]=0. Without an intercept, Cov(xⱼ,e)=−E[xⱼ]E[e] can be nonzero. An intercept makes E[e]=0 and hence makes these covariances zero; correlation is defined only for coordinates and residuals with positive variance, so correlation with the constant regressor is undefined. Neither cross-moment nor covariance orthogonality generally implies E[e|x]=0. A coefficient's units are outcome units per unit of its regressor, holding the other included coordinates fixed in the linear predictor.

For n observations, let X be the n×p matrix with rows xᵢ′ and y the outcome vector. If X has full column rank, ordinary least squares (OLS) gives β̂=(X′X)−1X′y. The fitted vector is Hy, where H=X(X′X)−1X′ is symmetric and satisfies H²=H; the residual vector is ê=My with M=I−H. The normal equations X′ê=0 follow directly. Expanding the sample objective around β̂ proves its unique minimum exactly as above. Rank failure leaves fitted values uniquely projected onto the column space but generally leaves coefficient coordinates unidentified; numerical inversion cannot resolve this.

Partial regression, derived. Partition X=[Z,W], where Z has full rank and [Z,W] has full rank. For any coefficient b on W, minimizing over the coefficient on Z gives residual MZ(y−Wb), with MZ=I−Z(Z′Z)−1Z′. Differentiate its squared norm: W′MZWb=W′MZy. Thus the W coefficient is obtained by regressing the residualized outcome MZy on residualized regressors MZW. The Gram matrix is positive definite: if MZWa=0, Wa belongs to the span of Z, contradicting full rank unless a=0. This is an algebraic statement about a common sample and common weights. It does not justify controlling for a post-treatment outcome or assigning causal meaning to the coefficient.

The population projection and partial-regression framework is developed in the scoped MIT linear-model notes. Our finite examples and proofs distinguish projection orthogonality from conditional exogeneity.

Worked example 1: a different weight asks a different question

A service's activity index Z takes −1, 0 and 1 with equal probabilities; its cost is deterministically Y=2+Z+Z² CU. The regressor is x=(1,Z)′. The three outcomes are 2, 2 and 4. Here EZ=0, EZ²=2/3 and EZY=2/3, so the unweighted projection is

β=(8/3,1)′, with residuals (1/3,−2/3,1/3).

The residual has zero mean and zero Z-weighted mean, but its conditional mean given Z is the displayed nonzero residual. The linear approximation does not equal the conditional mean function. No intervention, assignment mechanism or causal equation has been stipulated.

Now weight a central observation four times as much as either endpoint: w(−1)=w(1)=1, w(0)=4. The target minimizes E[w(Z)(Y−a−bZ)²]. Weighted symmetry still gives b=1, but the intercept is E[wY]/E[w]=7/3. The new residuals are (2/3,−1/3,2/3); their weighted sums, not their unweighted sums, vanish. The intercept difference −1/3 is a changed estimand, not finite-sample bias around the old intercept. Weighting is useful only after specifying which loss, population or conditional-mean model makes that target appropriate.

2. Exact conditional OLS and known-covariance GLS

Now impose a different model: y=Xβ+u, with full-rank X, E[u|X]=0 and Var(u|X)=Σ, a known symmetric positive-definite n×n matrix. Treat the following statements as conditional on X; for a fixed design, the conditioning is unnecessary. Then β̂−β=(X′X)−1X′u gives exact unbiasedness and

Var(β̂|X)=(X′X)−1X′ΣX(X′X)−1.

With Σ=σ²I this reduces to σ²(X′X)−1. Under unequal variances or correlated errors it generally does not. Population projection orthogonality alone does not imply E[u|X]=0 for the realized random design, so the exact unbiasedness assertion must not be silently transferred to every random-design projection.

Whitening and GLS. The spectral theorem supplies the symmetric matrix Σ−1/2. Multiply the model by it: y*=X*β+u*, where y*=Σ−1/2y, X*=Σ−1/2X and Var(u*|X)=I. Ordinary least squares on this transformed model is generalized least squares (GLS):

β̂G=(X′Σ−1X)−1X′Σ−1y,
Var(β̂G|X)=(X′Σ−1X)−1.

Efficiency proof and its comparison class. A linear estimator Ay is unbiased for every β exactly when AX=I. Put AG=(X′Σ−1X)−1X′Σ−1 and D=A−AG. Then DX=0 and DΣAG′=DX(X′Σ−1X)−1=0. Expanding the covariance therefore gives

AΣA′−AGΣAG′=DΣD′ ⪰ 0.

For every contrast c, its variance difference is (D′c)′Σ(D′c)≥0. Equality for that contrast holds exactly when D′c=0; equality of the whole covariance requires D=0. This is efficiency among linear unbiased estimators under the stated covariance, not among every conceivable biased estimator. OLS is the special efficient choice under spherical covariance. A positive-definite working covariance defines a weighted estimator but does not inherit efficiency when it differs from the true covariance.

Worked example 2: precision weights can make estimation worse when reversed

Three independent devices measure the same mean μ in CU. Their known error variances are 1, 4 and 9 CU²; a realized reading is y=(2,4,8)′. The only regressor is an intercept. OLS uses weights (1/3,1/3,1/3), giving 14/3 and exact variance 14/9. Correct GLS normalizes inverse variances:

aG=(36,9,4)/49, μ̂G=20/7,
Var(μ̂G)=36/49, Var(μ̂OLS)−Var(μ̂G)=362/441.

A mistaken program gives more weight to less precise devices: aW=(1,4,9)/14. Its weights still sum to one, so it remains unbiased in this model. But its estimate is 45/7 and its true variance is (1+64+729)/196=397/98, greater than 14/9. The observed closeness of any one estimate to an unknown μ cannot establish efficiency; the comparison uses the sampling covariance under the declared model.

3. When t and F are exact

Assume, in addition, u|X∼N(0,σ²I), σ²>0, n>p and full rank. Choose an orthonormal basis for the column space of X and extend it to an orthonormal basis of ℝⁿ. The density of u/σ is proportional to exp(−‖z‖²/2); an orthogonal change of coordinates has absolute determinant one and preserves that norm. Its coordinates are therefore independent standard normals. The fitted part Hu and residual part Mu use disjoint sets of these coordinates and are independent.

The residual sum of squares SSE=ê′ê=u′Mu has SSE/σ² equal to a sum of n−p independent squared standard normals, by definition χ²n−p. For a nonzero contrast c, c′(β̂−β)/[σ√{c′(X′X)−1c}] is standard normal and uses only fitted coordinates. With s²=SSE/(n−p), independence gives

t={c′β̂−c′β}/√{s²c′(X′X)−1c} ∼ tn−p.

Here tν is defined as Z/√(V/ν) for independent Z∼N(0,1), V∼χ²ν. This derivation proves the finite conditional law, rather than applying a degrees-of-freedom label to an arbitrary standard error.

For q linearly independent restrictions Rβ=r, let C=R(X′X)−1R′, positive definite because R has row rank q. The matrix B=C−1/2R(X′X)−1X′ satisfies BB′=Iq, and its rows belong to the fitted subspace. Extend those rows to an orthonormal basis of that subspace and then of ℝⁿ. The same density argument proves that, under the null, C−1/2(Rβ̂−r)/σ=B(u/σ) has independent standard normal coordinates and is independent of the residual sum of squares. Consequently

F={(Rβ̂−r)′C−1(Rβ̂−r)/q}/s² ∼ Fq,n−p,

where F is the ratio of independent chi-square variables divided by their degrees of freedom. For q=1, this F equals the squared t statistic. Non-Gaussian homoskedastic errors need not have independent fitted and residual parts. Heteroskedasticity also breaks this particular spherical decomposition. A robust standard error with a t critical value is not made exact by the notation. If Σ=σ²Ω with known positive-definite Ω, the same proof applies after whitening by Ω−1/2; replacing Ω by an estimate needs another argument.

4. Iid projection inference and residual-based sandwich covariance

Return to the population projection model. Let (xᵢ,yᵢ) be iid, p fixed, Q=E[xx′] positive definite, and impose the convenient sufficient moment condition E[(‖x‖+|y|)4]<∞. This is stronger than the weakest possible theorem; it makes every bound below transparent. Set eᵢ=yᵢ−xᵢ′β, gᵢ=xᵢeᵢ and Ω=E[gᵢgᵢ′]. Projection gives Eg=0 even when E[e|x]≠0. Since |e|≤max(1,‖β‖)(‖x‖+|y|), every fourth-degree product below is bounded by a constant times (‖x‖+|y|)⁴. In particular E‖x‖⁴, E‖x‖²e² and E[‖x‖³|e|] are finite.

Write Qₙ=n−1X′X. Entrywise iid laws of large numbers give Qₙ→PQ. Define β̂ and its covariance estimate as zero if Qₙ is singular; the probability of this event tends to zero by continuity of inversion near Q. This convention makes the asymptotic random sequences defined everywhere; an applied report should flag rank failure. On the nonsingular event the exact identity is

√n(β̂−β)=Qₙ−1n−1/2Σgᵢ
⇒ N(0,V), where V=Q−1ΩQ−1.

The iid centered score has finite second moment, so Chapter 1's scalar-contrast CLT and finite-dimensional characterization apply. Its normalized sum is OP(1), giving δ=β̂−β=OP(n−1/2). No conditional-mean-zero assertion or homoskedasticity was needed for this projection limit.

Residual replacement proof. With êᵢ=eᵢ−xᵢ′δ, estimate Ω by Ω̂=n−1Σxᵢxᵢ′êᵢ². The true-error average converges to Ω entrywise by its integrable LLN. In a compatible matrix norm the replacement error satisfies

‖Pₙ[xx′(ê²−e²)]‖≤2‖δ‖Pₙ[‖x‖³|e|]+‖δ‖²Pₙ‖x‖⁴=oP(1).

Both sample averages on the right are OP(1) by the explicit moment assumptions, and stochastic-order products finish the proof. Thus V̂=Qₙ−1Ω̂Qₙ−1→PV. The covariance estimate for β̂ itself is V̂/n, commonly called HC0:

ĈHC0=(X′X)−1[Σxᵢxᵢ′êᵢ²](X′X)−1.

For a fixed c with c′Vc>0, (c′β̂−c′β)/√(c′ĈHC0c)⇒N(0,1). Define the statistic arbitrarily on nonpositive estimated-variance events; consistency makes them negligible. This proves pointwise asymptotic inference at the declared law. It neither supplies exact finite-n coverage nor uniform coverage over nearly singular designs, changing dimensions or infinite-moment models. Ω and V can be singular; a zero-variance contrast cannot use this studentization.

Leverage and corrections. Leverage hᵢ=xᵢ′(X′X)−1xᵢ is H's ith diagonal. Since H is an orthogonal projection, 0≤hᵢ≤1 and Σhᵢ=p. HC1 multiplies HC0 by n/(n−p). HC2 replaces êᵢ² with êᵢ²/(1−hᵢ); HC3 uses êᵢ²/(1−hᵢ)². These require n>p and, for HC2/HC3, hᵢ<1. Under the iid assumptions,

max hᵢ≤‖Qₙ−1‖·max‖xᵢ‖²/n
≤‖Qₙ−1‖(Σ‖xᵢ‖⁴)1/2/n=OP(n−1/2).

Thus the correction multipliers converge uniformly to one, and their covariance estimates have the same probability limit as HC0. For this limit statement, assign zero covariance on undefined HC2/HC3 samples; the bound shows their probability tends to zero. Operationally, flag the failed leverage condition. This is an asymptotic equivalence result. Under the exact spherical model E[êᵢ²|X]=σ²(1−hᵢ), so HC2 removes this particular residual-square shrinkage in expectation. That fact does not create an exact t law under general heteroskedasticity. If an indicator identifies only one observation, its leverage can be one and its fitted residual is always zero; that observation's error variance cannot be learned from that zero.

Worked example 3: a complete finite sandwich calculation

Take xᵢ=(1,zᵢ)′, z=(−2,−1,1,2) and y=(0,2,2,8) CU. This is a realized dataset, not by itself a sampling model. Since Σz=0 and Σz²=10, β̂=(3,8/5)′. The residuals are (1,3,−13,9)/5 and SSE=52/5. The leverages are (13/20,7/20,7/20,13/20).

ĈHC0=[[13/20, 8/25], [8/25, 253/1250]].
s²=26/5; the homoskedastic slope-variance estimate is 13/25,
while the HC0 slope-variance estimate is 253/1250.

For example, the HC0 slope entry is Σzᵢ²êᵢ²/(Σzᵢ²)²=(4+9+169+324)/(25·100)=253/1250. The covariance entry is Σzᵢêᵢ²/(4·10)=8/25. HC0 need not exceed the homoskedastic estimate; neither is a samplewise upper bound. Whether either produces justified inference depends on the sampling model. Replacing z by ten times z divides the slope by ten, its variance by one hundred and the intercept–slope covariance by ten; fitted values and an appropriately stated t statistic are unchanged.

5. A feasible weighting theorem with actual score control

It is not enough to say that an estimated n×n covariance matrix is “consistent.” We prove a tractable finite-group case. Let iid observations include a category H∈{1,…,J}, with fixed finite J and P(H=h)>0. Suppose y=x′β+e, E[e|x,H]=0 and Var(e|x,H)=vh for positive finite constants vh. Impose the previous fourth-moment condition and Q positive definite. The weighted population Gram Qw=E[w(H)xx′], w(h)=1/vh, is positive definite because the finitely many weights have a positive minimum.

Start with OLS and define v̂h=Σ1{Hᵢ=h}êᵢ²/Σ1{Hᵢ=h}. LLNs give the denominator divided by n a positive limit, and the true-error numerator divided by n tends to P(H=h)vh. Expanding ê²−e² and bounding by 2‖δ‖Pₙ[‖x‖|e|]+‖δ‖²Pₙ‖x‖² shows the residual replacement is oP(1). Hence v̂h→Pvh. On samples with an absent group or nonpositive v̂h, define all weights as one; these exceptional events have probability tending to zero. Otherwise put ŵh=1/v̂h.

The feasible estimate solves ΣŵHᵢxᵢ(yᵢ−xᵢ′b)=0. Its weighted Gram converges to Qw, since the finite weight errors multiply group Gram averages OP(1). Crucially, the score perturbation is also controlled:

n−1/2Σ(ŵHᵢ−wHᵢ)xᵢeᵢ
=Σh=1J(ŵh−wh)n−1/2Σ1{Hᵢ=h}xᵢeᵢ=oP(1).

Each group score is centered by conditional exogeneity and is OP(1) after normalization by √n; finite J and consistency of each weight suffice. Independence between weight estimates and scores is not needed. Thus feasible and oracle estimators have the same first-order law, with Ωw=E[w²xx′e²]=E[wxx′]=Qw and root-n variance Qw−1.

More generally, estimates converging to a fixed finite list of positive working weights have root-n sandwich Qw−1ΩwQw−1 under the same group-centered score assumptions. The residual-based plug-in uses ŵ² in the meat and ŵ in the Gram. Their replacement errors vanish by the finite-group weight bounds and the iid residual argument. Efficiency is not guaranteed for wrong weights. Under conditional-mean misspecification, even group scores may have nonzero means: the preceding oP(1) score calculation then fails. Fixed weights can target a different βw, as in Worked example 1, and estimating them can have its own first-order influence. We make no generic oracle-equivalence assertion in that setting. The distinction between GLS, feasible weighting and robust covariance is discussed in the scoped Cameron–Miller treatment.

Worked example 4: learning two precision levels

Independent invoices come equally often from two processing categories. Their outcomes are y=μ+e, where e is a fair ±1 in category A and a fair ±3 in category B, independently across invoices. The categories are observed; the conditional mean is the same μ. Thus vA=1, vB=9, and OLS root-n variance is 5. Inverse-variance weighting gives Qw=(1+1/9)/2=5/9 and root-n variance 9/5. These are variances of √n times estimation error, so divide them by n for first-order variances of the estimated mean.

Estimating the two variances with the group residual averages satisfies every condition just proved: finite support, positive group probabilities and positive variance limits. At finite n a missing group or a zero residual variance can occur; the specified fallback makes the procedure defined and does not turn its finite-sample distribution into the oracle distribution. If category B instead has conditional mean μ+2, unequal weighting estimates a different weighted mean unless the regression includes a correctly specified category term. A robust variance estimate does not undo that change of target.

6. Clusters: sum the scores before squaring

Let the independent observations now be entire clusters Zg=(mg,Xg,yg), g=1,…,G, iid across g. Within-cluster dependence is unrestricted. Assume 1≤mg≤M for a fixed M; p is fixed; E[(Σj≤m_g(‖xgj‖+|ygj|))4]<∞; and Qc=E[Σjxgjxgj′] is positive definite. Define β to minimize E[Σj(ygj−xgj′b)²]. This is the pooled-row loss per cluster; with variable cluster sizes it is not the average of cluster-specific mean losses.

Write egj=ygj−xgj′β and Ug=Σjxgjegj. The normal equations give EUg=0. Whole-cluster moment bounds give E‖Ug‖²<∞. With Q̂c=G−1ΣXg′Xg, the exact expansion and iid cluster CLT are

√G(β̂−β)=Q̂c−1G−1/2ΣUg
⇒N(0,Vc), Vc=Qc−1E[UgUg′]Qc−1.

To estimate the middle matrix, use G−1ΣÛgÛg′, where Ûg=Xg′êg. Let Ag=Σ‖xgj‖² and Bg=Σ‖xgjegj‖. The difference from the true-score middle matrix has norm at most 2‖δ‖PG(AgBg)+‖δ‖²PGAg². Fourth moments and Cauchy–Schwarz make these averages OP(1), while δ=OP(G−1/2). This proves residual replacement and covariance consistency with independent-cluster normalization.

ĈCR0=(X′X)−1[ΣgÛgÛg′](X′X)−1=V̂c/G.

Squaring each row score and then summing drops the within-cluster cross products. A positive-variance contrast is asymptotically normal when studentized by CR0 under these hypotheses as G→∞. Counting N=Σmg rows as independent gives a different claim. Multiplying by G/(G−1)·(N−1)/(N−p) is a common finite-sample correction when defined; it tends to one here. It does not prove exact coverage, and a tG−1 reference is not a general exact law. Fixed G with growing cluster sizes, common shocks across clusters, or a single dominant cluster are outside this theorem. The primary cluster-inference review explains the importance of the independent cluster count and the limitations of small-cluster corrections; it supplies no universal safe cutoff.

Worked example 5: four teams are four independent common shocks

Each team has two measurements ygj=μ+ag+εgj. Team shocks are fair ±3; individual shocks are fair ±1; all generating shocks are independent except for the shared a within a team. Each row has variance 10 and within-team covariance 9. The pair score at μ is U=2a+ε₁+ε₂, with variance 38. Since Qc=2, the grand mean has exact variance 19/(2G). Treating 2G rows as independent gives 5/G, which omits 9/(2G).

Consider the possible four-team centered dataset (4,2), (−2,−4), (4,4), (−4,−4). Its grand mean is zero. The team score sums are 6, −6, 8 and −8, with squared sum 200; the row squared sum is 104. Therefore CR0 for the estimated mean is 200/8²=25/8, whereas HC0 is 104/8²=13/8. The true mean variance at G=4 is 19/8. Neither realized estimate must equal the truth or bound it.

For this intercept-only equal-size iid cluster model, CR0=(1/G²)Σ(ȳg−ȳ)². Its expectation is (G−1)/G times Var(ȳ), so multiplication by G/(G−1) removes that expectation bias. Independence and equal-size cluster means justify this special calculation. Their nonnormal finite distribution still does not supply an exact t law. Acquiring more independent teams and acquiring more measurements from the same teams answer different precision questions.

7. Serial dependence: a bounded theorem proved from blocks

We now work with a two-sided strictly stationary sequence Wt=(xt,yt), t∈ℤ. m-dependence means that the sigma-fields generated by {Wt:t≤a} and {Wt:t≥a+m+1} are independent for every integer a. The integer m is fixed. Assume ‖xt‖+|yt|≤K almost surely for one finite deterministic K, p fixed, and Q=E[xx′] positive definite. Define β as the population projection; et=yt−xt′β and gt=xtet are bounded, stationary, m-dependent and centered. This is a sufficient finite-range model, not a description of every economic time series.

For any centered scalar bounded m-dependent sequence zt, covariance vanishes when indices differ by more than m. For any finite set A of indices,

Var(Σt∈Azt)≤(2m+1)B²|A| when |zt|≤B.

There are at most 2m+1 potentially nonzero covariance partners per term, each bounded in absolute value by B². Consequently bounded sample averages satisfy a Chebyshev weak law. This applies to each Gram entry, hence Qₙ→PQ. Let Γℓ=E[gtgt−ℓ′]. Direct covariance expansion gives

Var(n−1/2Σgt)=Γ₀+Σℓ=1min(m,n−1)(1−ℓ/n)(Γℓ+Γℓ′)→ΩLR,
ΩLR=Γ₀+Σℓ=1m(Γℓ+Γℓ′).

The limit is positive semidefinite as a limit of covariance matrices. Covariance convergence alone is not a CLT; the next argument supplies the missing distributional result.

Separated-block proof for a scalar contrast. Fix c and set zt=c′gt. Take blocks of ℓₙ=⌊n1/3⌋ consecutive observations, separated by m omitted observations. Drop the final incomplete block as well. The retained block sums Bnj are mutually independent: each successive block is independent of the sigma-field containing all previous retained blocks. The number rₙ of omitted indices is O(nm/ℓₙ+ℓₙ+m)=o(n). The preceding variance bound gives E[(Σomittedzt/√n)²]≤C rₙ/n→0. Thus omission is negligible in L² and probability.

The retained sum's variance divided by n has the same limit σc²=c′ΩLRc as the full sum: the difference is bounded by the omitted variance and twice the square root of the product of full and omitted variances, after division by n. The full normalized variance is bounded. If σc²=0, the full normalized sum tends to zero in L² and the contrast has a degenerate limit.

For σc²>0, put ξnj=Bnj/√n and vnj=Eξnj². Define the deterministic envelope bₙ=Bℓₙ/√n. Then max|ξnj|≤bₙ almost surely, bₙ→0, Σvnj→σc² and max vnj≤Cℓₙ/n→0. Replace each independent ξ by an independent centered normal ζ with the same variance. For a bounded C³ test function h with bounded derivatives, a third-order remainder after the quadratic term gives a total replacement error at most

(‖h‴‖∞/6)Σ[E|ξnj|³+E|ζnj|³]
≤Ch[bₙ+√(max vnj)]Σvnj→0.

The first two terms cancel because means and variances match and each inserted variable is independent of the others. For a centered normal of variance v, its third absolute moment is v3/2E|Z|³, finite by its density. The sum of the ζ's is exactly normal with variance Σvnj. Its smooth-test expectation converges to that of σcZ: the absolute difference is at most ‖h′‖∞|√(Σvnj)−σc|E|Z|. To turn smooth convergence into CDF convergence, use decreasing smooth transitions q(s)=1−35s⁴+84s⁵−70s⁶+20s⁷ on [0,1], extended as one to the left and zero to the right. Its first three derivatives match at the endpoints, and q′=−140s³(1−s)³≤0. The shifted functions q((t−a+ε)/ε) and q((t−a)/ε) bound I{t≤a} from below and above. First take n→∞ and then ε↓0; continuity of the positive-variance normal CDF squeezes the probabilities to the normal limit. This proves the scalar block CLT without importing an independent triangular-array theorem.

Apply the already identified finite-dimensional Cramér–Wold characterization from Chapter 1 to all contrasts. The OLS identity then yields √n(β̂−β)⇒N(0,Q−1ΩLRQ−1) and β̂−β=OP(n−1/2). Boundedness and fixed m are substantive restrictions. We have not established these conclusions from covariance summability alone, for arbitrary mixing sequences, persistent common shocks or growing dimension.

8. Bartlett covariance: positivity, consistency and inference are separate

For integer 0≤L<n, use fitted score vectors ĝt=xtêt and a common denominator n:

Γ̂ℓ=n−1Σt=ℓ+1nĝtĝt−ℓ′,
Ω̂B=Γ̂₀+Σℓ=1L(1−ℓ/(L+1))(Γ̂ℓ+Γ̂ℓ′).

This heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation covariance estimator uses Bartlett weights. The scoped MIT HAC notes give the formula and long-run covariance interpretation. Their broader dependent CLT is not being assumed here. We prove positivity and consistency under the bounded finite-range model just established.

Finite-sample positive semidefiniteness. Extend ĝt by zero outside 1,…,n and let Hj=Σr=0Lĝj−r, j=1,…,n+L. In ΣHjHj′ a score's own square appears L+1 times; an ordered pair at distance ℓ≤L appears L+1−ℓ times. Therefore

Ω̂B={1/[n(L+1)]}Σj=1n+LHjHj′ ⪰ 0.

For any vector a the quadratic form is a sum of (a′Hj)² divided by a positive constant. This proof is exact for any finite score sequence, without a probability model. It does not prove that the estimate is close to the desired population covariance.

Consistency with an explicit sufficient bandwidth. Return temporarily to true scores g. For one lag ℓ, each centered product gtgt−ℓ′ is bounded and (m+ℓ)-dependent: index sets separated by more than m+ℓ are independent. Entrywise covariance counting gives Var(Γ̃ℓ)≤C(m+ℓ+1)/n, with a constant independent of n and ℓ. Also EΓ̃ℓ=(1−ℓ/n)Γℓ. Summing mean absolute deviations by Cauchy–Schwarz over all weighted lags bounds the stochastic error by C(L+1)√[(m+L+1)/n]. No independence across lag estimates is claimed or required.

For ℓ>m the population covariance Γℓ is zero. For the finitely many nonzero lags, the edge factors 1−ℓ/n tend to one; Bartlett factors tend to one if L→∞. Their total deterministic bias is O(1/(L+1)+1/n) once L≥m. Thus true-score Bartlett covariance is consistent if L→∞ and L³/n→0. This conservative rate is sufficient, not necessary.

Finally ĝt−gt=−xtxt′δ. Uniform boundedness of x and g bounds each residual-product replacement by C‖δ‖+C‖δ‖², uniformly over t and ℓ. Summing lags gives OP((L+1)/√n)=oP(1) under the same bandwidth rate. Hence Ω̂B→PΩLR. A concrete rule is Lₙ=min(n−1,⌊n1/4⌋). The usual sandwich Qₙ−1Ω̂BQₙ−1/n consistently estimates the first-order coefficient covariance, and a contrast with positive limiting variance is asymptotically normal after studentization by it.

Fixing L forever retains nonunit weights on nonzero lag covariances. It can produce a positive semidefinite but inconsistent estimate of the long-run variance. Conversely, a lag-window sum with unit weights might target the finite-range covariance if the correct range were known, yet be negative in a particular finite sample. Positivity, convergence to the right covariance and a valid distributional approximation are three separate checks.

Worked example 6: serial cost shocks and the bandwidth trap

Let ηt be iid fair ±1 for all integer t, and observe yt=μ+et with et=ηt+(1/2)ηt−1. This is a bounded stationary 1-dependent intercept model. Direct independence calculations give γ₀=5/4, γ₁=1/2 and zero other lag covariances. Therefore

ΩLR=9/4,
Var(ȳₙ)=9/(4n)−1/n²; at n=20 this is 11/100.

The iid variance shortcut γ₀/n gives 1/16 at n=20. With L=1, the Bartlett lag-one weight is 1/2, so its probability limit is γ₀+γ₁=7/4, not 9/4. With fixed L=2 the limit is 23/12; increasing a fixed lag count can improve this bias without making it vanish asymptotically. The growing bandwidth rule proved above removes that attenuation at this fixed law.

For a separate realized intercept residual sequence (1,−2,1), n=3, Γ̂₀=2, Γ̂₁=−4/3 and Γ̂₂=1/3. The untapered lag-one sum is −2/3 and cannot be a variance. Bartlett with L=1 gives 2/3, exactly equal to [1²+(−1)²+(−1)²+1²]/6 from the moving sums. Bartlett with L=2 gives 4/9. These small-sample arithmetic facts verify positivity; they are not evidence of coverage for a time-series law.

9. What a defensible regression report must identify

Report the target and its units, the sampling unit, the observation or cluster count, and the assumptions making scores centered. State whether the model conditions on X, treats rows as iid, treats whole clusters as iid, or imposes a specified time-series process. Disclose the covariance formula, corrections, clustering variable, lag rule and exceptional-event convention. A design with high leverage, few independent clusters or nearly collinear regressors can be unreliable even when a large file makes matrix multiplication easy.

Inference after searching many outcomes, cutoffs or specifications is a further problem; the fixed pre-specified contrast theorems do not automatically cover it. Serially correlated errors can coexist with endogenous regressors; HAC addresses the covariance only after the score's mean and projection target have been justified. If economic interpretation requires a structural parameter, articulate the intervention, exclusion or assignment restrictions separately. Robust inference is robustness to a stated class of covariance variation under maintained assumptions, not immunity to misspecification, selection or unidentified causality.

The companion source checker recomputes the original finite distributions, projections, exact covariance matrices and score sequences with standard-library rational arithmetic, checks bounded finite cases and validates displayed numbers. Run python3 scripts/check_v12_c02.py from the book directory, or invoke that file by absolute path from another directory; python3 -O is also supported. Success is quiet; check() returns a summary. Its finite checks do not prove the asymptotic theorems: the assumptions, remainder bounds and probability arguments require the separate mathematical reading recorded in the author review. The checker is part of the project source; the readable chapter and its solutions are included in the reader edition.

Exercises

Show the target, sampling assumptions, units and calculation. Problems 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10 contain proof tasks. Problem 12 is a research critique with an explicit rubric. None requires a theorem beyond the chapter and its stated prerequisites.

  1. For Worked example 1, derive both projection vectors directly from their normal equations. Calculate both losses at the unweighted and weighted minimizers under the unweighted loss. Explain why nonzero E[e|Z] does not contradict E[xe]=0 and why neither coefficient is a demonstrated causal effect.
  2. Recompute all three estimates and true variances in Worked example 2. Prove that any other linear unbiased estimator has covariance exceeding known-covariance GLS by a positive-semidefinite matrix, and characterize equality for a single contrast. Would replacing the true covariance by any positive-definite matrix preserve the proof's efficiency conclusion?
  3. For Worked example 3, reconstruct X′X, β̂, residuals, SSE, leverages and every HC0 entry. Calculate the HC2 slope-variance entry. Then rescale z to z*=10z: give the new slope, HC0 slope variance and intercept–slope covariance. Explain which inferential assertions can and cannot be made from these four realized observations alone.
  4. Prove the iid HC0 residual-replacement result under the stated fourth-moment assumptions, including why its two bounding sample averages are OP(1). Show why HC2 and HC3 have the same limit under those hypotheses. For X with rows (1,0),(1,0),(1,1), calculate all leverages and explain why dividing every residual square by 1−hᵢ is not an everywhere-defined rule.
  5. Under the conditional Gaussian spherical model, derive the independent components that give exact t and F, and prove F=t² for one restriction. Then take n=2 independent observations yᵢ=μ+εᵢ with fair εᵢ∈{−1,1}. For any fixed finite positive k, find the exact coverage of [ȳ−ks/√2,ȳ+ks/√2], where s²=Σ(yᵢ−ȳ)² and a zero-width interval is used when s=0. Does homoskedasticity alone imply the Gaussian exact law?
  6. Modify Worked example 4 so category A occurs with probability 1/4 and has fair errors ±2, while B occurs with probability 3/4 and has fair errors ±4. Find OLS and oracle weighted root-n variances. Prove the group residual-variance estimates are consistent and that using their inverse weights changes the normalized score by oP(1). Identify exactly where conditional exogeneity enters; explain why consistency of weights alone does not prove oracle equivalence under mean misspecification.
  7. In the team model, compare 40 measurements arranged as 20 independent teams of two with 10 independent teams of four, retaining common shock ±3 and individual shocks ±1. Derive both true grand-mean variances and the erroneous row-independent variance. Recompute the displayed four-team HC0 and CR0 values. Show why the equal-size intercept correction G/(G−1) is unbiased for variance here but does not by itself establish exact confidence coverage.
  8. Independent clusters are of two equally likely types: type A contains one row with y=0, and type B contains three rows all with y=4. Only an intercept is fitted. Derive the pooled-row target, the equal-cluster-mean target, and the root-G variance of each estimator. Separately, with one team and indefinitely many individual measurements in the ±3 common-shock model, prove failure of consistency for μ. Explain which condition of the bounded-size iid-cluster theorem each change tests.
  9. Supply the essential details of the bounded m-dependent CLT: the omitted-index count, the variance bound for omitted sums, mutual independence of retained blocks, and vanishing total third-order replacement error. Explain how smooth tests yield a CDF result. Then set et=ηt−ηt−1 with iid fair signs. Find its long-run variance and the exact sample-mean error; explain why a zero long-run variance does not mean every finite-sample estimate is error-free.
  10. Prove the zero-extension moving-sum identity for Bartlett covariance, including the edge multiplicities. For residuals (1,−2,1), compute Γ̂₀, Γ̂₁, Γ̂₂, untapered L=1 and Bartlett L=1 and L=2. In the stated consistency proof, which powers Lₙ=⌊na⌋ satisfy all sufficient bounds? Does failure of that particular bound at a=1/3 prove inconsistency?
  11. Change the moving-average coefficient in Worked example 6 from +1/2 to −1/2. Derive γ₀, γ₁, the long-run variance, the exact n=20 mean variance and the fixed-L=1 Bartlett probability limit. Compare the direction of the iid variance error with the original case. State which properties would need new proofs if the process were unbounded or had dependence extending through infinitely many lags.
  12. A report regresses outcomes on a service-adoption indicator and controls using one million customer-month rows from eight firms. It weights each firm by its inverse estimated residual variance, reports HC3 with a t critical value, chooses the model with the smallest p value among twenty specifications, and concludes that the coefficient is a causal effect with exact 95% coverage because “robust standard errors handle any dependence.” Write a methodological audit separating the target, score centering, independent units, estimated weights, finite-sample reference and specification selection. Give two feasible evidence or design changes and what each would resolve. No current institutional fact is assumed.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. The unweighted normal equations are a=EY=8/3 and bEZ²=EZY=2/3, hence b=1. Weighted equations give aEw=EwY with Ew=2 and EwY=14/3, so a=7/3; symmetry gives b=1 again. At the unweighted solution, mean squared residual is (1+4+1)/27=2/9. At the weighted solution, the unweighted mean square is (4+1+4)/27=1/3. The increase is (−1/3,0)Q(−1/3,0)′=1/9, agreeing with the projection decomposition. For the first solution, E[e]=0 and E[Ze]=0 by direct summation, but conditioning on each Z reveals residuals 1/3,−2/3,1/3. A finite-dimensional orthogonality condition is weaker than a zero conditional mean function. Both are descriptive approximations to the supplied joint law; no counterfactual or assignment restrictions identify an intervention effect.
  2. OLS: (2+4+8)/3=14/3 and (1+4+9)/9=14/9. GLS: normalize (1,1/4,1/9) to (36,9,4)/49; estimate (72+36+32)/49=20/7 and variance (1296+324+144)/2401=36/49. Wrong weights: (2+16+72)/14=45/7 and (1+64+729)/196=397/98. The OLS–GLS difference is 362/441>0. In general AX=I and AGX=I imply DX=0. Since ΣAG′=X(X′Σ−1X)−1, both covariance cross terms vanish and the difference is DΣD′. Positive definiteness makes c′DΣD′c=0 exactly when D′c=0. A wrong working covariance W changes AG to AW; the analogous product DΣAW′ need not vanish with the true Σ. The explicit wrong-weight variance already refutes universal efficiency.
  3. X′X=diag(4,10); X′y=(12,16)′ gives (3,8/5)′. Residuals (1,3,−13,9)/5 have zero sum and zero z-weighted sum. Their squared sum is 260/25=52/5, and hᵢ=1/4+zᵢ²/10 gives (13/20,7/20,7/20,13/20). HC0's entries are SSE/16=13/20, (−2−9+169+162)/(25·40)=8/25 and (4+9+169+324)/(25·100)=253/1250. HC2's slope entry is [328/(25·(7/20))+178/(25·(13/20))]/100=1102/2275. Rescaling gives slope 4/25, HC0 slope variance 253/125000 and covariance 4/125; the intercept remains 3. Fitted values and residuals stay fixed. These are exact numerical estimators for the realized data; their bias, precision or coverage needs a sampling law and the hypotheses of an applicable theorem. The smaller HC0 number does not certify a stronger result.
  4. Set δ=β̂−β. The exact score expansion and iid finite-second-moment CLT give δ=OP(n−1/2), since Qₙ tends to a nonsingular Q. The identity ê²−e²=−2ex′δ+(x′δ)² and ‖xx′‖=‖x‖² yield the displayed bound. E‖x‖⁴ is finite by assumption, and ‖x‖³|e|≤max(1,‖β‖)(‖x‖+|y|)⁴ gives an integrable bound. The same bound with a different constant controls ‖x‖²e², since e=y−x′β. Their averages converge by the integrable LLN and are OP(1). The true meat entries are integrable by E‖x‖²e²<∞, proving consistency. Also max hᵢ≤‖Qₙ−1‖(Pₙ‖x‖⁴)1/2/√n→0. Hence the maximum absolute difference between either HC2/HC3 multiplier and one tends to zero on events with max hᵢ<1/2. Multiplying by the tight average Pₙ‖x‖²ê² proves equal limits; exceptional samples become negligible. In the three-row design X′X=[[3,1],[1,1]], inverse [[1/2,−1/2],[−1/2,3/2]], giving h=(1/2,1/2,1). The last row is fitted exactly. Its zero residual divided by zero is undefined; a procedure must reject or explicitly handle that design, not claim the variance is zero.
  5. An orthonormal basis splitting span(X) from its complement transforms u/σ into independent standard normal coordinates because the spherical density and unit absolute Jacobian are unchanged. A normalized fitted contrast uses only the first p coordinates, while SSE/σ² is the sum of squares of the remaining n−p. Their independence gives t. For q restrictions, whiten R(β̂−β) by C−1/2/σ: it has identity covariance, a joint normal density and independent coordinates, all independent of the residual sum. Its squared norm divided by q and the independent residual mean square give F. For one restriction the numerator quadratic form is the square of the normalized scalar contrast, so the ratio equals t². In the two-sign example, with probability 1/2 both errors have the same sign: ȳ=μ±1, s=0, and the singleton interval misses μ. With probability 1/2 signs differ: ȳ=μ, s²=2, and every positive-k interval covers. Exact coverage is therefore 1/2 for every stated k. Homoskedasticity holds, but the non-Gaussian errors invalidate the normal-coordinate argument.
  6. OLS root-n variance is (1/4)4+(3/4)16=13. The weighted Gram for an intercept is Qw=(1/4)(1/4)+(3/4)(1/16)=7/64, giving variance 64/7. For each group the observation fraction tends to its positive probability. The true-error squared numerator divided by n tends to that probability times its conditional variance. The OLS residual-square difference is bounded by terms proportional to |δ|Pₙ|e|+δ² for this intercept model, which vanish by consistency and finite moments. Ratio continuity proves v̂h→vh; positivity follows with probability tending to one. The normalized score perturbation equals Σh(ŵh−wh)n−1/2Σ1{Hᵢ=h}eᵢ. Conditional mean zero makes each inner sum centered with bounded variance, hence OP(1); the finite weight errors are oP(1). This is the required product proof, despite using the same data for weights. Under misspecification a group score mean can be nonzero, making its normalized sum grow at rate √n. Mere weight consistency then supplies no oP(1) conclusion, and fixed weights can already change the target.
  7. For G teams of common size m, a team's mean has variance 9+1/m, and the grand mean has variance (9+1/m)/G. Thus 20 pairs give 19/40, while 10 teams of four give 37/40. Each row has variance 10, so the false independence calculation gives 10/40=1/4 in both designs. For the displayed four pairs, score squares sum 36+36+64+64=200, row squares sum 104 and N²=64: CR0=25/8 and HC0=13/8. Let Vb=Var(ȳg). Independence gives EΣ(ȳg−ȳ)²=(G−1)Vb. CR0 divides this by G², whereas Var(ȳ)=Vb/G; multiplying by G/(G−1) is therefore unbiased. It does not establish independence of ȳ and its variance estimate or a Gaussian numerator. Those missing distributional properties, not an expectation correction, govern exact t coverage.
  8. Pooled OLS is Σmgȳg/Σmg, targeting E[mȳ]/Em=(.5·0+.5·12)/2=3. The equal-cluster-mean average targets Eȳ=(0+4)/2=2. At pooled target 3, cluster score is −3 in type A and +3 in type B, so Qc=Em=2, Ωc=9 and root-G variance 9/4. The equal-cluster estimator averages iid values 0 and 4, with variance 4. Both are consistent for their own targets; size-dependent outcomes prevent identifying them with one another. With one team, ȳₘ−μ=a+ε̄ₘ tends to a=±3 by the iid law for individual shocks, and |a+ε̄ₘ|≥2 for every m. It never approaches zero in probability. The first example respects bounded iid clusters but changes loss weighting and its estimand. The second fixes the independent cluster count and lets size grow, outside the theorem; row growth is not G→∞.
  9. With ℓ=⌊n1/3⌋, there are at most n/ℓ separating gaps of length m and a final remainder shorter than ℓ+m, so r≤mn/ℓ+ℓ+m=o(n). In any omitted set, at most 2m+1 covariance terms per row are nonzero and each is bounded in absolute value, giving normalized omitted variance ≤Cr/n→0. The gap makes each new retained block independent of the sigma-field of all earlier ones; recursion gives mutual independence. Retained variance tends to the full long-run variance by Cauchy–Schwarz with the L²-small omission. Normalized block sums satisfy max|ξ|≤bₙ almost surely for the deterministic bₙ=Bℓ/√n→0, ΣEξ²=O(1), and max Eξ²≤Cℓ/n→0. Hence ΣE|ξ|³≤bₙΣEξ²→0. Matching normal variables obey ΣE|ζ|³≤E|Z|³√(max Eξ²)ΣEξ²→0. Taylor replacement cancels first and second terms and bounds the remaining expectation error. The smooth decreasing q transitions bound each CDF event; take n→∞ then transition width to zero at the continuous positive-variance normal law. A zero limiting variance instead uses Chebyshev directly. For the differenced-sign process, γ₀=2, γ₁=−1 and ΩLR=0. The mean error telescopes to (ηₙ−η₀)/n, with exact variance 2/n² and positive probability of nonzero error. Its root-n limit is zero because that scale loses the remaining endpoint randomness, not because the estimator is always exact.
  10. For a fixed score index t, windows j=t,…,t+L include it, giving L+1 occurrences. For t and s with t−s=ℓ∈{1,…,L}, the overlap has L+1−ℓ windows. Zero extension includes the truncated edge windows without changing these multiplicities. Expanding ΣHjHj′ and dividing by n(L+1) therefore gives exactly the symmetric Bartlett formula, and every contrast is a sum of squares. The three residuals give Γ̂₀=6/3=2, Γ̂₁=(−2−2)/3=−4/3 and Γ̂₂=1/3. Untapered L=1 is 2−8/3=−2/3; Bartlett L=1 is 2−4/3=2/3; L=2 is 2+(4/3)(−4/3)+(2/3)(1/3)=4/9. The proven requirements L→∞, L³/n→0 and L/√n→0 hold for 0<a<1/3. At a=1/3 the conservative stochastic-error upper bound does not vanish. An inconclusive upper bound is not a lower bound on error, so it does not prove inconsistency; a sharper argument could permit more bandwidths.
  11. With e=η−η−1/2, γ₀=1+1/4=5/4 and γ₁=−1/2, so ΩLR=1/4. Direct finite covariance summation gives Var(ȳₙ)=1/(4n)+1/n², or 3/200 at n=20. The iid calculation remains 1/16, now too large rather than too small. Fixed-L=1 Bartlett tends to γ₀+γ₁=3/4, exceeding the correct 1/4. Negative covariance can reduce variance; ignoring dependence has no universal conservative direction. Unbounded observations invalidate the uniform block and residual-product bounds as written and need replacement moment/tail conditions. Infinite-range dependence invalidates independent separated blocks and the finite covariance-bias argument; it requires a new dependence CLT and lag-tail/estimation controls. A familiar covariance formula alone supplies none of those missing theorems.
  12. Illustrative audit and rubric, 12 points. Award two points each for six explicit distinctions: (i) define a population descriptive or intervention estimand and explain that adoption selection and controls do not themselves identify a causal effect; (ii) justify score centering for that target, rather than infer it from sample normal equations; (iii) identify possible within-firm serial, customer and common cross-firm dependence, so one million rows and eight firms do not establish an iid-row or G→∞ approximation; (iv) state that estimated inverse-variance weights need stable Gram and centered group-score control and may change a misspecified projection target; (v) distinguish HC3's leverage adjustment and asymptotic scope from the exact conditional Gaussian t proof, with no universal few-cluster guarantee; and (vi) identify the selected minimum p value as outside a pre-specified single-contrast test. Each distinction earns one point for the issue and one for its consequence or needed evidence. Feasible changes include a documented randomized service rollout with a defined treatment contrast and outcome calendar, which can address assignment but not automatically dependence; obtaining substantially more independent firms under a defensible sampling design, which addresses cluster information but not confounding; pre-specifying or holding out the outcome/model choice with a justified selection-aware procedure; and auditing the category-mean/covariance model before weighting. At least two changes must be connected to their limited purpose. Other defensible audits receive credit; “use robust errors” or “collect more rows” alone does not answer the question.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why the same normal-equation algebra can lead to three different covariance estimators. Derive which products must be preserved for iid rows, independent teams and serial scores. Then explain why changing weights can change the target while changing only the covariance estimator does not change β̂.

Teach-back answer

The coefficient error is an inverse sample Gram times an average score. Its covariance depends on which score cross products survive under the sampling model. Iid rows use E[gg′]; independent clusters use E[(Σ within-cluster g)(Σ within-cluster g)′], retaining within-cluster products; serial data use the long-run sum of lag covariances, together with a justified dependent CLT and consistent lag estimation. Their effective normalizations are √n, √G and √n under the separate hypotheses proved here. Replacing a covariance formula leaves the original minimizer unchanged. Replacing loss weights alters the normal equations and generally the population minimizer, unless a common correctly specified conditional mean makes each weighted score centered. Neither operation supplies a causal design.

Delayed check, after 7–14 days. Without the text: two independent devices have variances 1 and 4; find the OLS and GLS variances and GLS weights. For et=ηt+(1/3)ηt−1 with iid fair signs, find γ₀, γ₁, long-run variance and the fixed-L=1 Bartlett limit. State the positive-variance and bandwidth requirements needed for our serial studentization result. The delay is an authored practice suggestion, not an empirically calibrated guarantee.

Retention answer and repair route

OLS has variance (1+4)/4=5/4. GLS weights are (4/5,1/5), giving variance 4/5. For the serial model γ₀=10/9, γ₁=1/3 and ΩLR=16/9; fixed-L=1 Bartlett instead tends to 13/9. A positive limiting variance is required for the contrast's division, and the bounded stationary fixed-m theorem uses L→∞ with L³/n→0, also ensuring residual error L/√n→0. For a wrong weight target revisit Sections 1 and 5; for a missing within-cluster covariance, Section 6; for confusing finite positivity with consistency, Sections 7–8; for an exact-t overclaim, Section 3. Reconstruct the calculation with a changed covariance sign to test transfer rather than memorization.

Sources, limits and next study

The source record uses only the inspected portions of the MIT linear-model notes, Cameron–Miller's author-hosted cluster-inference article, and the MIT HAC notes. Those sources support the projection, working-weight and covariance framework; our cases, finite comparisons, explicit sufficient moment/rate choices, bounded blocking proof, consistency bounds and exercises are original. The primary Newey–West paper was a discovery lead whose body was unavailable in the source preparation; no original-paper proof inspection is claimed. No source's empirical example or problem bank is reproduced.

We proved exact linear-unbiased efficiency for known covariance, exact t/F only under the stated Gaussian model, iid fixed-dimensional HC consistency, finite-group feasible-weight equivalence with centered group scores, iid bounded-size cluster inference and bounded fixed-m serial inference with a conservative bandwidth rate. General mixing, long-memory, growing or dominant clusters, many regressors, weak-rank sequences, small-cluster refinements, post-selection inference and fully general feasible covariance estimation require further theory. Numerical reproduction verifies finite examples, not these general proofs. The next chapter studies instruments and moment conditions: a covariance estimator can quantify uncertainty around an identified score equation, but it cannot manufacture the missing identifying restriction.

Sources and further study

Projection framework only; Sections1 and4. The fixed-dimensional proof is supplied in the chapter, not inherited from unspecified growing-dimensional regularity.
  • A. Colin Cameron and Douglas L. Miller — A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference — Conditional covariance and cluster-score sandwich; averaging over independent clusters; known-covariance GLS versus estimated weighting; covariance-model-dependent efficiency; robust inference with a working covariance; few-cluster bias and critical-value limitations. Known versus working covariance and cluster-score covariance framework; Sections2,5,6. Exact efficiency, finite-group score limits and bounded-size cluster proof independently supplied.
  • Victor Chernozhukov and Ivan Fernandez-Val — 14.382 Spring 2017 Lecture 4: Euler Equations, Nonlinear GMM, and Other Adventures — Long-run covariance as the sum of score autocovariances; Bartlett weights 1-lag/(L+1), common denominator n and symmetric lag terms; explicit dependence and moment assumptions for a stated CLT. Long-run covariance and Bartlett lag formula; Section8. The chapter supplies its own finite PSD and bounded finite-range consistency/CLT proofs.
